title: How to diagnose OutOfMemoryError: check which area ran out (Heap space, Metaspace, unable to create native thread), take heap dump, analyze for large object retention or memory leaks?

s1_definition.oneliner: Read the OOM message first to learn which region ran out, then take a heap dump and find what is retaining the memory.
s1_definition.profdef: OutOfMemoryError (OOM) is thrown when the JVM cannot allocate memory and the garbage collector cannot free enough to satisfy the request. The first diagnostic step is reading the error's message to learn which region ran out, because each points to a different cause: "Java heap space" means the heap is exhausted, "Metaspace" means class metadata exhausted, "unable to create new native thread" means the OS could not create another thread, and "GC overhead limit exceeded" means GC is running constantly while freeing almost nothing. You then capture a heap dump and analyze it in Eclipse MAT for large object retention or a leak.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I hit an OutOfMemoryError, the very first thing I do is read the error message, because it tells me which region of memory ran out, and each region points to a completely different cause and fix. If it says "Java heap space," the heap is full of live objects, which means either a genuine need for a bigger heap, a memory leak, or a request that tried to load far too much into memory at once. If it says "Metaspace," class metadata is exhausted, which almost always means a class-loader leak from things like proxy generation or repeated redeployments. If it says "unable to create new native thread," it is not a heap problem at all; the operating system refused another thread, usually because of a thread leak or an OS limit, since every thread needs a native stack outside the heap. And "GC overhead limit exceeded" is an early warning of a heap problem, where GC is running almost constantly while freeing almost nothing.

Once I know the region, I take a heap dump and analyze it. In production I always run with heap-dump-on-OutOfMemoryError and a dump path set, so the JVM captures a full snapshot at the exact moment of failure instead of losing the evidence. I open that dump in Eclipse Memory Analyzer, where the Dominator Tree shows which objects retain the most memory and the path to GC roots shows exactly what is holding them alive. I also correlate with the GC logs to tell whether the heap baseline was drifting up slowly, which signals a leak, or spiked suddenly, which signals a bad request.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, I have diagnosed all three of these. Our reporting service crashed with "Java heap space" because a report tried to load an entire year of transactions into one list, and the heap dump made it obvious with a single giant list dominating memory, so we fixed it by streaming and paginating instead. On the same app server, after many redeployments, we hit "Metaspace" from leaked class loaders, which we bounded with MaxMetaspaceSize so it failed fast and alerted. And a batch job that spawned a thread per account instead of using a pool failed with "unable to create new native thread," which we fixed with a bounded thread pool. The habit that saves me every time is to read the message first and never just raise the heap size, because that only delays a leak instead of fixing it.

Remember one sentence: How to diagnose OutOfMemoryError: check which area ran out (Heap space, Metaspace, unable to create native thread), take heap dump, analyze for large object retention or memory leaks is fundamental knowledge for Java interviews and production banking work.

---

keyPoints: Heap OOM: capture heap dump, analyze with MAT, find leak
Metaspace OOM: too many classes loaded – check classloader leaks
Direct buffer OOM: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, check NIO buffer usage
GC overhead limit: GC spending >98% time recovering <2% memory
Stack OOM: too many threads – reduce thread count or increase -Xss
